recall.question: What does this guide tell you before you start Volume 1?
recall.answer: It tells you the study order, the daily pace of 4+ hours, how the volumes connect, and how one big project connects all parts.

recall.question: What are the three things you can do when you finish the curriculum?
recall.answer: Explain how an LLM is built end to end, think like a researcher, and ship like an engineer from notebook to production.

recall.question: What does the 'think like a researcher' promise require?
recall.answer: Read a paper and extract its real claim, design an experiment with baselines and ablations, and know what a result proves and does not prove.

sections.title: 2. Study order and the dependency graph

keyTerms.definition: The nesting order of volumes; each volume assumes the previous ones.
The image for the curriculum: each volume rests on the one inside it.

The finish line of a phase; a phase ends when its milestone holds.

recall.question: Why must you not skip ahead in the volume order?
recall.answer: Each volume assumes you read the previous ones and teaches concepts once. Skipping leaves you meeting terms with no definitions, like KL divergence in Volume 7.

recall.question: What are the five phases and their order?
recall.answer: Foundation (volumes 1-3), core build (4-8), production (9-10), research (11-12), review (13-14).

recall.question: When is a phase done?
recall.answer: When its milestone holds. Milestones beat calendars; a phase ends at its milestone, not when the week ends.

sections.title: 3. Pacing: Work more than 4 hours each day.

keyTerms.definition: At day's end, explain the hardest idea aloud from memory in simple words.
Work 50 minutes, take a 10-minute break; four blocks fill the 4-hour day.

recall.question: What is the daily study plan?
recall.answer: Hour 1-2: read one chapter carefully and trace the examples. Hour 3: do the lab and break one thing on purpose. Hour 4: DSA track or a paper. Bonus: speak the hardest idea aloud.

recall.question: Why is the re-explanation rule the most effective habit?
recall.answer: Reading is not learning. If you cannot explain the hardest idea from memory in simple words, you do not know it yet.

sections.title: 4. Build an LLM (large language model) from scratch. This is the capstone project.

keyTerms.definition: One tiny LLM built volume by volume; each lab reuses the last volume's artifact.
Byte-pair encoding: the algorithm that divides text into pieces.
Supervised fine-tuning: training on example answers.
Direct preference optimization: training from human preferences.
Stored key-value memory that makes generation fast.
Shrinking the number precision of the model.

recall.question: What does the capstone produce by Volume 8?
recall.answer: One tiny model built end to end across volumes 1-8. You have touched every stage of the LLM lifecycle and can explain each stage.

recall.question: What breaks if a handoff fails?
recall.answer: Fix a broken artifact at once, because later labs build on it. Nothing is rebuilt from zero.

keyTerms.definition: The climb every chapter follows: simplest model, mechanism, full picture.
The design question each chapter answers; cover the answers and quiz yourself.
Run the code, change one variable, observe, break one thing on purpose, repeat until it clicks.
Memory drops steeply in the first day unless you retrieve it.

recall.question: What are the four gates of 'done' for a chapter?
recall.answer: Define every term in plain words, work the example numbers yourself, explain the diagram to another person, and answer the design prompts aloud.

recall.question: What are the four moves of the lab loop?
recall.answer: Run the code unchanged and save one good run, change one variable, write down what changed, break one thing on purpose then fix it.

recall.question: Why does the re-explanation rule sit at the end of every study day?
recall.answer: The forgetting curve drops steepest in the first 24 hours. Retrieval resets the curve; spaced effort beats re-reading.

keyTerms.definition: Data structures and algorithms studied 1-2 hours daily, parallel to the spine.
Name the pattern and learn its template before solving problems with it.

recall.question: What is the rule for the DSA track?
recall.answer: Patterns before problems. Learn the pattern template, solve 2-3 problems with the pattern, then move to the next pattern.

recall.question: How does the DSA track relate to the spine?
recall.answer: It runs alongside the spine, never inside it: 1-2 hours a day from the Top-300 path while the volumes run.

keyTerms.definition: The ordered volume sequence; the spine decides when a module opens.
What a module is: consult it, not a second curriculum.

recall.question: When should you open a module you already own?
recall.answer: Only when a volume points to it; read the named chapter only, then return to the spine. Curiosity is not a pointer.

recall.question: Which module is the core of Volume 9?
recall.answer: The RRK Agentic AI Textbook v2 plus Interview QA Bank v2, covering agents, RAG, evals, guardrails, and GPU infra basics.

keyTerms.definition: Five gates that stay closed: no skipping math, run the code, one volume at a time, honest markers, generic and portable.
Believe a volume when it says a number is illustrative or a treatment is first-principles.

recall.question: What are the five ground rules?
recall.answer: No skipping the math, run the code instead of just reading, one volume at a time with its capstone lab, honest markers on illustrative numbers, and generic portable files with no personal information.

recall.question: Where do you start after this guide?
recall.answer: Start with Volume 0 of the crash pack, then read Volume 1: Math for ML first, in order, with the DSA track open from day one.
